RagShortTexts: Aachen served as the historic imperial coronation venue housing Charlemagne's sacred marble.

Variants.Content: The Palatine Chapel at Aachen went up between about 786 and 805 under Charlemagne, with its central octagon modelled on San Vitale in Ravenna. Columns and marble were salvaged from older Roman and Byzantine sites. From the coronation of Otto I in 936 onward, German kings were usually crowned here rather than in Rome. The rite set the new king on Charlemagne's marble throne after the Archbishop of Cologne had anointed him, so each coronation renewed a claim to the Carolingian inheritance. The relics and treasury kept in the chapel also made Aachen a pilgrimage and revenue centre, and every crowning gave the city and its chapter a chance to press their privileges on the new monarch.

Aachen answered to the crown alone, so a territorial prince could not tax its baths or seize its markets without an imperial letter. Canons of the Cologne church expected lodging at each coronation and drew rents from nearby estates. A sealed royal writ could settle a rent dispute faster than any local levy, so a careful baron kept a clerk in the city and watched who was winning the king's favour.
